response.text:
Using the standard Rayleigh data table with 8 observations in each group, let

\[
\mu_C=\text{mean mass for chemical-compound nitrogen},\qquad
\mu_A=\text{mean mass for atmospheric nitrogen},
\]

and define the difference as

\[
\Delta=\mu_A-\mu_C.
\]

The sample summaries are

\[
\bar x_C=2.2994725,\qquad s_C=0.0013792,\qquad n_C=8,
\]

\[
\bar x_A=2.3102988,\qquad s_A=0.0005539,\qquad n_A=8.
\]

Thus

\[
\widehat{\Delta}=\bar x_A-\bar x_C
=2.3102988-2.2994725
=0.0108263.
\]

---

## (1) Test for a difference in means

We test

\[
H_0:\mu_A-\mu_C=0
\]

against

\[
H_1:\mu_A-\mu_C\neq 0.
\]

Using Welch’s two-sample \(t\)-test,

\[
T=\frac{\bar x_A-\bar x_C}{\sqrt{s_A^2/n_A+s_C^2/n_C}}.
\]

The standard error is

\[
SE=\sqrt{\frac{0.0005539^2}{8}+\frac{0.0013792^2}{8}}
\approx 0.0005255.
\]

Therefore

\[
t=\frac{0.0108263}{0.0005255}\approx 20.60.
\]

The Welch–Satterthwaite degrees of freedom are approximately

\[
\nu \approx 9.20.
\]

So the two-sided p-value is

\[
p=2P(t_{9.20}\ge 20.60)\approx 5\times 10^{-9}.
\]

Thus the p-value is extremely small. We reject \(H_0\) at any conventional significance level. There is overwhelming evidence that the mean mass differs between the two sources. Since \(\bar x_A>\bar x_C\), atmospheric nitrogen appears heavier on average.

---

## (2) 95% confidence interval for the mean difference

A 95% Welch confidence interval for

\[
\Delta=\mu_A-\mu_C
\]

is

\[
\widehat{\Delta}\pm t_{0.975,\nu}SE.
\]

With \(\nu\approx 9.20\),

\[
t_{0.975,9.20}\approx 2.26.
\]

Hence

\[
0.0108263\pm 2.26(0.0005255)
=
0.0108263\pm 0.001185.
\]

Therefore the 95% CI is approximately

\[
\boxed{(0.00964,\;0.01201)}.
\]

So atmospheric nitrogen is estimated to have mean mass about \(0.0108\) grams per flask larger than nitrogen from chemical compounds, with a 95% confidence interval of roughly \(0.0096\) to \(0.0120\) grams.

If the difference is defined oppositely, \(\mu_C-\mu_A\), the interval is

\[
\boxed{(-0.01201,\;-0.00964)}.
\]
